title: Political notes: ‘Flowers’ for the living, cupcakes for the interim birthday caucus
summary: The farewell celebrations continue as the session nears the end, retiring from the House of Delegates comes with more than just some flowers and kind words and the large, but so far unseen, Interim Birthday Caucus gets its day, in political notes.
content:
by Rhiannon Evans and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

by Rhiannon Evans and William J. Ford, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

At most workplaces, it wouldn’t be unusual for a retiring colleague to get a bouquet of flowers, some kind words and maybe some applause. At the workplace that is the Maryland House of Delegates, you can get your bills revived as well as a parting gift.

That was the case Friday for an emotional Del. Susan McComas (R-Harford), a member of the House for 24 years who is retiring after her legislative term is up this year.

“I just didn’t feel like I had the juice to run again,” McComas said of her decision to retire, emotion thick in her voice. “And I didn’t want to go out losing as opposed to winning. But I am so honored to have been elected six times.”

The Republican started her legislative career as a file clerk in Wyoming and joked that she has more credibility in the Western state than she does in Maryland. She said it makes her sad that there’s no center in politics, which is why she thinks some of her bills have stalled this session.

“I’ve also got this very limited bill that they don’t understand in Economic Matters. It’s an appeal bill!” McComas said to a roar of laughter from the delegates. “So anyway, if anyone wants to treat me with a bill, please! God help me, yes!”

After House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Anne Arundel and Prince George’s) joked that no bill is dead until Sine Die, Del. Marc Korman (D-Montgomery), chair of the Environment and Transportation Committee, stepped in to save the day.

“Speaking of which, I’d like to move the delegate from Harford County’s HB 1301 from the Economic Matters Committee to the Environment and Transportation Committee,” he offered.

McComas was not the only retiring lawmaker honored by her colleagues this week, but she was the only one to see a bill revived. For Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince  George’s), Del. Anne Healey (D-Prince George’s) and Del. Barrie Ciliberti (R-Frederick), the parting gift of choice seemed to be having a bill renamed in their honor.

Ciliberti was honored again during Satuday’s special session, along with Del. Pam Queen (D-Montgomery), who received citations for their service in the chamber.

Ciliberti, who turns 90 in July, is the oldest member of the General Assembly and will not seek reelection this year.

First elected in the GOP sweep of 1994, when Democrat Parris Glendening was governor, he was unseated four years later and spent 16 years out of office before being elected to House again in 2014, when Republican Larry Hogan was governor. He has remained in the House since.

“If I had known this was coming, I wouldn’t have shown up,” Ciliberti said from the rostrum to some laughs in the chamber. “I better end this [speech] before I have tears.”

As for Queen, she has been in the House of Delegates since 2016 when first appointed. She was elected two years later.

Del. Anne Kaiser (D-Montgomery) read prepared remarks about Queen, who has a doctorate in finance and is an associate professor at Morgan State University. Kaiser also highlighted Queen’s battle with breast cancer, and how she helped craft bills on mammograms and critical screenings that would be available for women statewide.

“She is a leader who turned her personal trials into public triumphs. She understood that policy is personal,” Kaiser said.

Queen gave every woman in the chamber a letter to “think about the things that are important to us.”

“It’s been a great honor to serve with all of you,” said Queen, who has served under three House speakers. “Sometimes you know when it’s time to leave. I’m one of those people who know, it’s time to go.”

Del. Mary Lehman (D-Prince George’s) on Saturday revealed the existence of what is easily the largest caucus in the House: the interim birthday caucus, made up of delegates who celebrate birthdays outside the 90-day legislative session.

Lehman, who celebrates her birthday this month, said about three-quarters of the members have birthdays that aren’t between early January and the middle of April.

She desiganted the remaining time for Dels. Lily Qi (D-Montgomery) and April Miller (R-Frederick) to take turns reading portions of an interim birthday caucus resolution.

In one part of the resolution, laughter erupted in parts of the chamber from this line read by Qi: “And whereas, it is inherently unfair that a delegate born in February receives a standing ovation, while a delegate born in November, like me, receives only a notification from their dentist, and if they’re nice, maybe a birthday card from Sen. [J.B.] Jennings, or our speaker pro tem.”

Here’s the last two sentences from the resolution read by Qi and Miller.

“And be it further resolved, that for the purpose of this resolution and all members born between mid-April and early January, are hereby granted constructive birthday status allowing them to feel as special as the session-born members, provided that they do not actually try to claim an extra year of seniority,” Miller said.

“And be it further resolved, that the House actually officially recognizes that while some members’ birthdays may occur during the interim, their presence in this chamber remains mostly tolerated, and on this day, collectively celebrated,” Qi said.

After some applause in the chamber, Pena-Melnyk said, “Thank you for gifting us a little joy.”

In the chamber’s lounge, a table full of cupcakes with toothpicks in each holding the photo of one of the members who celebrate their birthdays in the interim.
